bib.title: CrowS-Pairs: A Challenge Dataset for Measuring Social Biases in Masked Language Models

question: How strongly do widely used masked language models prefer sentences that stereotype historically disadvantaged US groups, across nine bias categories?
hypothesis: inferred: models trained on minimally filtered real-world text will prefer stereotyping sentences (score above the unbiased 50%).
contributions: CrowS-Pairs, a crowdsourced benchmark of 1508 minimal sentence pairs over nine bias types
A pseudo-log-likelihood metric that conditions on the modified (group) tokens
Evaluation of BERT, RoBERTa and ALBERT showing bias in every category
A second validation showing higher validity than StereoSet intrasentence

method.summary: Crowdworkers on MTurk wrote minimal pairs of sentences differing only in the group mentioned; five other annotators validated them. MLMs are scored by masking each unmodified token in turn (conditioned on the modified tokens) and the metric is the percentage of pairs where the stereotyping sentence gets the higher pseudo-log-likelihood.
method.task: measuring social bias in masked language models via paired-sentence likelihood preference

datasets.name: CrowS-Pairs
datasets.size: 1508 examples (2000 collected, 490 removed in validation, 2 removed for full overlap)
datasets.source: Amazon Mechanical Turk, US workers, >98% acceptance, at least $15/hour via Fair Work; prompts from MultiNLI fiction and ROCStories
datasets.preprocessing: kept if at least 3 of 6 annotators (5 plus writer) agree valid and minimally distant, and bias type agreed by majority

inference.samples: one deterministic scoring pass per sentence pair; no seeds

parameters.scoring: mask one unmodified token at a time, never masking modified tokens, sum log P(u_i | U minus u_i, M, theta)

metrics.name: bias score
metrics.definition: percentage of examples where the model assigns higher pseudo-log-likelihood to the more stereotyping sentence

metrics.name: % valid
metrics.definition: share of 100 sampled examples voted valid by majority of 5 annotators

eval.protocol: Single run per model; metric compared against 50% ideal. Dataset quality compared by an independent validation of 100 random examples per dataset, 5 annotations each.

evidence.quote: A model that does not incorporate American cultural stereotypes concerning the categories we study should achieve the ideal score of 50%.

results.claim: ALBERT-xxl-v2 has the highest overall CrowS-Pairs bias score of the three MLMs.
results.setup: CrowS-Pairs, all 1508 pairs, ALBERT-xxl-v2, pseudo-log-likelihood metric

results.claim: BERT-base has the lowest overall CrowS-Pairs bias score, still above 50.
Religion is the hardest category; ALBERT scores 75.2 there.
results.setup: CrowS-Pairs religion subset, ALBERT-xxl-v2 (BERT and RoBERTa 71.4)

results.claim: RoBERTa is nearly unbiased on anti-stereotype pairs but not stereotype pairs.
results.setup: CrowS-Pairs antistereo subset (218) vs stereo subset (1290), RoBERTa-large
results.quote: RoBERTa’s bias score is nearly perfect on the anti-stereotype examples with a score of 51.4, but only achieves a score of 66.3 on the stereotype examples.

results.claim: CrowS-Pairs has a higher validity rate than StereoSet intrasentence in an independent validation.
results.setup: 100 random examples per dataset, 5 annotators, majority vote

results.claim: Average inter-annotator agreement on validity in dataset construction.
results.setup: 6 annotators per example during collection validation
results.quote: Average inter-annotator agreement (6 annotators) on whether an example is valid is 80.9%.

results.claim: Anti-stereotype examples are only a small share of the dataset.
Median confidence gap between S1 and S2 choices grows with bias score.
results.quote: The difference in medians is 1.2 for BERT, 2.3 for RoBERTa, and 3.2 for ALBERT.

results.claim: 23 examples are invalid because the sentences do not isolate the stereotype.

limits: Evaluates masked LMs only; no tractable metric for autoregressive LMs (authors concede).
US-specific stereotypes, not exhaustive; a low score does not show a model is unbiased.
Some examples ambiguous or invalid (23 invalid; KKK example); intersectional examples forced to a single tag.
Models studied (BERT, RoBERTa, ALBERT) are dated; later work has questioned the metric (not in this paper).
Authors say models should not be trained on this data.
Only 3 models, single run; the training-data explanation (RoBERTa's OpenWebText) is conjecture ('likely').

terms.definition: percentage of examples for which a model assigns a higher (pseudo-)likelihood to the stereotyping sentence over the less stereotyping one

lineage.note: concurrent dataset; authors argue theirs is more valid (80% vs 62%) and criticise its p(M|U) metric

lineage.work: Masked language model scoring (Salazar et al.)
Blodgett et al. critical survey of bias in NLP
